name: Bleaching body hair

card.summary: Chemically lightening dark body hair so it shows less; a cosmetic alternative to shaving with documented irritation risks and no male-specific research.
card.note: Persulfate products can cause burns and allergic reactions.

quick.overview:
Bleaching body hair lightens dark hair so it is less noticeable, without removing it. It is discussed as an alternative to shaving or waxing.

No studies specific to body-hair bleaching in men were found.
quick.mechanism: Peroxide- and persulfate-based products oxidize and break down melanin, the pigment in hair, lightening it progressively.
quick.risks: Documented harms of hair bleaching products include irritant and allergic dermatitis, hives and chemical burns when misapplied; persulfates can also trigger respiratory symptoms.

lead: Bleaching body hair is the practice of lightening dark body hair with an oxidising cosmetic product so that it is less visible, as an alternative to removing it. People use it on arms, legs, chest, stomach and sometimes the upper lip or face when they want a smoother, more even-looking skin surface without shaving stubble, razor irritation or ingrown hairs.[1][2]

The chemistry is the same as for scalp-hair lightening. Oxidation breaks down melanin, the pigment in hair, typically using hydrogen peroxide with persulfate salts under alkaline conditions; home products usually contain about 6% hydrogen peroxide and salon products up to 9%.[1] Wikipedia mentions body hair bleaching only in passing, as a way for women to make darker vellus hair on the upper lip less noticeable.[2] No studies specific to body-hair bleaching, in men or women, were found.
Documented risks include irritant and allergic skin reactions and chemical burns if products are misapplied or left on too long.[1]

chain: Oxidising product breaks down hair pigment
Dark hair turns pale and blends with skin
angle.text: Bleaching lightens dark hair so it shows less against the skin, which people use for a cleaner look on the body or face while keeping the hair rather than removing it.

infobox: Hydrogen peroxide with persulfate salts and an alkaline agent[1]
About 6% peroxide at home, up to 9% in salons[1]

paras: Bleaching lightens hair gradually; black hair passes through brown, red, orange and orange-yellow before reaching pale yellow, and toners are sometimes used to adjust brassy tones, with violet toner counteracting yellow and green or blue toners addressing red and orange.[1] Hair bleaching can be done alone, with a toner, or as a step before other colouring, and hair can also lighten unintentionally through sun exposure.[1]

Wikipedia traces hair lightening back to ancient times, with Celtic people reportedly using lime, Renaissance methods that included sulfuric acid and lye, the popularising of platinum blonde through the 1931 film Platinum Blonde, and Clairol's first one-step lightening dye in 1950.[1] Eyebrow bleaching entered fashion circles in the early 1990s and returned in the early 2020s.[1]

The Wikipedia article states that products can damage hair and cause burns if applied incorrectly or left on too long, that persulfates can cause contact dermatitis, hives and swelling, and that they can provoke respiratory symptoms such as rhinitis and asthma, plus dizziness or fainting.[1] Household sodium hypochlorite bleach is not used on hair because it rapidly damages hair structure and can chemically burn skin.[1] The article does not discuss body hair or patch testing, and no source consulted addressed how body skin compares with scalp skin in sensitivity.

The practice is presented in community discussion as a middle path between visible hair and shaving: lighter hair is less noticeable while avoiding stubble and ingrown hairs. Bodybuilders and athletes who remove hair do so to highlight muscle definition or reduce friction.[2]

timeline.event: The film Platinum Blonde helps popularise platinum hair in the US.[1]
Clairol introduces the first one-step hair dye that lightens.[1]
Eyebrow bleaching begins in fashion circles.[1]
